questions.q: Why might VARCHAR fail to reliably store certain real-world names?
options: VARCHAR uses roughly one byte per character, which isn't enough for characters outside basic English letters/digits/punctuation
VARCHAR has no length limit and always causes errors
VARCHAR can only store numbers
VARCHAR is deprecated in modern SQL Server
questions.explain: Accented letters, Cyrillic, Chinese, Japanese, and other scripts often can't be represented reliably in plain VARCHAR.

questions.q: What does NVARCHAR(n) provide that VARCHAR(n) doesn't?
options: Unicode support, capable of representing virtually every written language's characters
A larger maximum length limit
Automatic trimming of trailing spaces
Faster query performance in all cases
questions.explain: NVARCHAR behaves like VARCHAR (variable length) but stores characters using Unicode encoding.

questions.q: What is the storage tradeoff of using NVARCHAR instead of VARCHAR?
options: NVARCHAR generally uses about twice the space per character
NVARCHAR uses less space than VARCHAR
There is no storage difference between the two
NVARCHAR requires exactly double the declared length limit
questions.explain: Unicode storage costs roughly double per character — real overhead, but usually worth it for international text.

questions.q: What does the N prefix on a string literal do, e.g. N'José'?
options: Marks the literal as Unicode, so it's interpreted correctly rather than through the server's default non-Unicode code page
Converts the string to uppercase
Declares the string as NULL
Limits the string to numeric characters only
questions.explain: Without the N prefix, special characters in a literal can be silently mangled by the server's default code page interpretation.

questions.q: When is it worth paying NVARCHAR's storage overhead?
options: For anything that might contain international names, addresses, or user-generated content — which is most real applications
Never — VARCHAR should always be preferred regardless of content
Only for numeric columns
Only when the column will never contain any text at all
questions.explain: The overhead is a reasonable cost to avoid data corruption or loss for real-world, potentially international text.
